items.title: Slide Hampton — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: I heard Ornette Coleman and Don Cherry, and I liked it.

ctx.x: What did you think about when the avant garde came?

I heard Ornette Coleman and Don Cherry, and I liked it. I liked what they were playing. The thing that I found might have been somewhat a problem with them: it seemed as though they didn’t feel as though they needed to keep working on the basic things of playing to keep progression in what they were playing. See, when Dizzy and them made the change, they were still working on the basics. They were still learning

scales. They were still working on chords and all that kind of thing. So that gave them something to go on. I think that Ornette and them, when they made their change, they didn’t relate to those things that came before. There was no part of what they did that you could hear any of that in. I could hear it in what they were playing, because I thought that they – they reminded me a lot of Dizzy and Bird when they came along, and I was thrilled with what they were doing. items.title: Slide Hampton interviewed by Monk Rowe, West Orange, New Jersey, July 30, 2003
items.q: free jazz and so forth, that Ornette was doing and some of Coltrane’s later work

ctx.x: Oh yeah. That orchestra I think Jimmy Owens had a great deal to do with that orchestra. And I got to write quite a few things for them. It was a wonderful experience because I was free to do whatever I wanted to, usually some kind of direction in the program, but it was a chance to have the freedom as far as the things that I wanted to try, the things that I wanted to experiment with and all of that. It was a wonderful opportunity for me so I think I had a chance to do a lot of good things there, to learn a lot…
What did you think of the — I guess they would have called it the avante garde period, free jazz and so forth, that Ornette was doing and some of Coltrane’s later work.

We did a lot of that in Europe already before I came back you know. In fact in Europe they had some subsidy for projects that were based on free music, that means that you were usually doing things that were somewhat unusual to the way that you usually approach composing or writing music. And I thought it was a thing that had a good effect on, in general, on our musical growth, because it was a chance for us to experience something different in music.
